sections.body: The AI Researcher covers how artificial intelligence is used across the research and teaching cycle, from finding and reading papers to running experiments and reviewing results. In practice, AI now helps search and summarize literature, extract claims from papers, map citations, suggest statistical methods, code data analysis, transcribe interviews, draft grant sections, check writing, generate course materials, manage research data, and control or simulate laboratory equipment. It also enters peer review through plagiarism checks, statistical checks, and reviewer matching, though human editors and reviewers still make decisions. The site library holds 135 research papers and 11795 claims extracted from research works, which shows the scale of text and evidence that these tools are being asked to handle. The work is not one technology but a mix of search, language models, machine learning, and data systems applied to scholarly tasks.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some parts are mature, such as citation lookup, reference formatting, plagiarism detection, and reproducible code for standard quantitative analysis. Other parts remain fragile, including literature synthesis that must judge quality, qualitative coding that depends on context, and peer review where confidentiality and accountability matter. AI can generate plausible text, but it can also invent citations, miss negative results, reproduce bias in training data, and fail on novel methods. Evaluation is hard because benchmarks rarely match real research workflows, and many tools are closed, so independent checking is limited. Governance is still catching up, with questions about authorship, disclosure, data privacy, and responsibility that institutions answer in different ways. The honest limit is that AI can assist with research and teaching tasks, but it cannot be trusted as an autonomous scholar or teacher.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader starts with Literature Review and Evidence Synthesis for search, screening, and summarization, then moves to Citation Mapping and Discovery to see how papers connect and how fields evolve. Quantitative Analysis and Reproducible Work covers statistics, code, and replication, while Qualitative Analysis and Mixed Methods deals with interviews, coding, and combining text and numbers. Grant Proposals and Funding looks at finding calls, writing proposals, and funder rules, and Academic Writing and Peer Review covers drafting, editing, journal checks, and reviewer workflows. Course Design and Teaching turns the same tools toward syllabi, assessments, and classroom support, and Research Data and Repositories handles data management, metadata, and sharing. Laboratory Automation and Simulation covers robots, instruments, and computational experiments, and Governance, Ethics and Research Integrity sets the rules that connect all the other pages. The site catalogue includes 91 AI books, 800 scientific models, 732 AI tools, and 686 glossary terms, so these pages can point to definitions, models, and tools without treating any one product as the answer.
